INTEREST OF AMICI1
The American Civil Liberties Union
(“ACLU”) is a nationwide, nonprofit organization
that, since 1920, has sought to protect the civil
liberties of all Americans, with 54 affiliates across the
United States. Established in 1965, the ACLU’s
Voting Rights Project (“VRP”) has worked to protect
the gain s in political participation for all citizens.
Since its inception,  VRP has litigated hundreds of
voting rights cases, including cases concerning the
potential disenfranchisement of eligible voters
through states’ list maintenance programs in violation
of the National Voter Registration Act of 1993
(“NVRA”). The ACLU has also appeared before this
Court as counsel or amicus curiae in numerous cases
involving electoral democracy, including Smith v.
Allwright, 321 U.S. 649 (1944), Reynolds v. Sims, 377
U.S. 533 (1964) , Thornburg v. Gingles , 478 U.S. 30
(1986), Citizens United v. Federal Election
Commission, 558 U.S. 310 (2010) , Department of
Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752 (2019), and Allen
v. Milligan, 599 U.S. 1 (2023).
The American Civil Liberties Unions of
Alabama (“ACLU -AL”), Arizona (“ACLU -AZ”),
Florida (“ACLU -FL”), Iowa (“ACLU -IA”), Texas
(“ACLU-TX”), and Virginia (“ACLU-VA”) are state

2
affiliates of the national ACLU . ACLU-AZ is a
statewide, nonprofit, nonpartisan organization with
over 20,000 members throughout Arizona who are
dedicated to protecting the fundamental liberties
guaranteed by the Constitution, including the right to
vote. ACLU-AZ has a strong interest in protecting the
ability of its members to vote and register to vote and
ensuring that Arizonans can fully engage in the
democratic process. ACLU -AL, ACLU-FL, ACLU-IA,
ACLU-TX, and ACLU -VA are also statewide,
nonprofit, nonpartisan organizations. They are
likewise dedicated to protecting the fundamental
liberties guaranteed by the Constitution, including
the right to vote, and have all witnessed the impacts
of error-prone voter removal programs in their states.
The ACLU and its affiliates listed herein frequently
file amicus curiae briefs on a wide range of civil
liberties and civil rights issues.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
The National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”)
serves and balances two important goals recognized
by Congress: increasing the number of eligible citizens
who are registered and who vote in federal elections
and keeping voter registration rolls accurate and
current. Section 8(c)(2) of the NVRA , 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2), effectuates these goals by  allowing
states to use systematic list maintenance programs to
keep voter rolls up to date and accurate, but requiring
states to complete those programs “not later than 90
days prior to” a federal election. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). That ninety-day window is known as
the “Quiet Period.”

3
In enacting this statute, Congress determined
that permitting states to engage in systematic voter
roll maintenance during the ninety-day Quiet Period
would carry an unacceptable  risk of disenfranchising
eligible voters. First, Congress understood that when
states run systematic programs to remove ineligible
voters from their voter rolls, they run a significant
risk of removing eligible voters as well. Second, an
eligible voter who is removed during the Quiet Period
is likely to experience significant difficulty in
correcting the error in time to cast a ballot. Third ,
Congress also r ecognized that systematic voter roll
maintenance programs operate on large numbers of
people at once; as a result, the difficulty in correcting
systematic errors is compounded as a potentially
larger number of  voters who have been mistakenly
removed from the rolls seek to correct those errors
during the voting period . In light of these problems,
Congress struck  a careful balance,  allowing
systematic removal programs most of the time and
prohibiting them only in the immediate lead-up to an
election, when the risk of disenfranchising eligible
voters is greatest. The Quiet Period also protects
against the inevitable confusion to voters that would
result if states systematically remov ed voters during
the Quiet Period, particularly when absentee and
early voting are already underway.
The issue here is not whether states may remove
noncitizens from their voter rolls ; everyone agrees
they may do that. Rather, the issue is whether eligible
citizens will bear the cost of a state’s mistakes when
there is too little time left to correct them. Congress
decided they should not.

4
Petitioner Republican National Committee
(“RNC”) urges this Court to recognize an exception to
the Quiet Period that would allow systematic
programs directed at noncitizens to run within the
ninety-day period. As discussed in Part I below, t hat
argument contradicts both the statute’s plain text and
its purpose. Section 8(c)(2)(A) reaches “any program”
whose purpose is to systematically remove ineligible
voters. It exempts only removals at the request of the
registrant, because of a criminal conviction or mental
incapacity, or because the registrant has died . 52
U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B)(i) (citing §§ 20507(a)(3)(A),
(a)(3)(B), & (a)(4)(A)). Those exceptions are exclusive.
The RNC attempts to graft onto the Quiet Period an
exception that Congress did not create.
Moreover, as amici explain in Part II below,
experience shows that the mistakes Congress
anticipated are real, and that systematic programs
aimed at noncitizens are especially prone to such
mistakes because they  rely on motor -vehicle, labor,
and federal records that are often outdated,
incomplete, or inaccurate. In Part III, amici set out
research demonstrating that it is exceedingly rare for
noncitizens to be on voter rolls, and even rarer for
them to actually vote.
Section 8(c)(2) is clear on its face: Congress forbids
the kind of systematic voter roll maintenance the RNC
and the United States support here. But even if their
policy arguments were relevant to the statutory
interpretation question here (and they are not) , the
empirical data supports the balance Congress actually
struck: It protects eligible voters from erroneous
removal on the eve of a federal election, while
addressing the very small risk of noncitizen voting, by

5
permitting states to conduct systematic programs at
any time other than during the Quiet Period and to
remove individuals from the rolls based on
individualized information  at any time, including
during the Quiet Period. The RNC, the United States,
and some of the RNC’s amici clearly disagree with
Congress’s judgment. But their policy arguments are
better directed at Congress itself, which spoke clearly
through the plain text of Section 8(c)(2).
ARGUMENT
I. THE QUIET  PERIOD PROVISION
EMBODIES CONGRESS’S DELIBERATE
APPROACH TO BOTH ENSURING
ELECTION INTEGRITY AND PROTECTING
VOTERS AGAINST DISFRANCHISEMENT.
The text of the  NVRA’s Quiet Period provision
plainly requires that states “complete, not later than
90 days prior to” a federal election , “any program the
purpose of which is to systematically remove the
names of ineligible voters from the official lists of
eligible voters .” 52 U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(A). The
statutory language is straightforward. The “word ‘any’
has an expansive meaning” that means “one or some
indiscriminately of whatever kind.” United States v.
Gonzales, 520 U.S. 1, 5 (1997) ; Ali v. Fed. Bureau of
Prisons, 552 U.S. 214,  219 (2008) (quoting Webster’s
Third New Int'l Dictionary 97 (1976)). Applying that
ordinary meaning to the Quiet Period provision, “any
program” captures all programs that seek to
“systematically remove the names of ineligible
voters.” 52 U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(A). “Any program ”
clearly encompasses a systematic program seeking to
remove noncitizens from the rolls.

6
Congress’s enumeration of exceptions to the Quiet
Period rule further underscores that states cannot
create others. Congress specified certain exceptions to
the Quiet Period provision, but none applies here.
Congress expressly provided that the  Quiet Period
statute “shall not be construed to preclude  . . . the
removal of names  from official lists of voters ” for
certain categories—namely, at the request of the voter
registrant herself, due to  criminal conviction or
mental incapacity, or due to death .” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(B)(i).2 That Congress “considered the
issue of exceptions and, in the end, limited the statute
to the ones set forth,” United States v. Johnson , 529
U.S. 53, 58 (2000), confirms the Quiet Period provision
does not admit any other,  unenumerated exceptions.

2 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii) contains a second caveat: that the
Quiet Period provision  “shall not be construed to preclude” the
“correction of registration records pursuant to this chapter.”
Neither the RNC nor the Respondents in support of the RNC rely
on this provision, and for good reason.  Section 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii)
refers to other provisions in chapter 205 of Title 52 of the U.S.
Code (chapter 8 of the NVRA) , in which Congress set out very
detailed requirements for list maintenance based on change of
residence, including the specific circumstances in which states or
registrants can “correct” their registration records. E.g., 52
U.S.C. §§ 20507(c)(1)(B)(i), (d)(1)(B)(ii), (d)(3), (e)(2)(A)(i),
(e)(2)(A)(ii)(I), (e)(2)(A)(ii)(II), (f). Thus, the Quiet Period
provision’s specific reference to “correction of registration records
pursuant to this chapter” merely makes clear that there is no bar
on such “corrections” of voter registration information during the
Quiet Period. See 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii). Moreover, on its
plain terms and consistent with these other provisions of the
NVRA, a “correction” under 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(1)(B)(ii) only
results in a change or update to an existing voter registration
record, and not removal from the voter rolls. Compare, e.g., 52
U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B)(i) (“removal”) with 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii) (“correction”).

7
“When Congress provides exceptions in a statute, it
does not follow that courts have authority to create
others.” Id.; see also Keene Corp. v. United States, 508
U.S. 200, 208 (1993)  (courts have a “duty to refrain
from reading a phrase into [a] statute when Congress
has left it out”); Va. Uranium, Inc. v. Warren, 587 U.S.
761, 765 (2019) (“it is our duty to respect not only what
Congress wrote, but, as importantly, what it didn’t
write”). “[E]xpressing” those exceptions, as Congress
did, “excludes [others] left unmentioned,” Esteras v.
United States , 606 U.S. 185, 195 (2025)  (citation
modified)—including the noncitizen list maintenance
exception the RNC seeks here.
Nor is there any other basis to read the statutory
text as excepting systematic programs aimed at
removing people who are ineligible based on lack of
U.S. citizenship . The RNC  contends that Section
8(c)(2) bars only programs that seek to remove voters
who were eligible at the time of registration  but
became ineligible at some later point. RNC Pet’r’s
Br. 41–42. And, it says, noncitizens are not “ineligible
voters” because they  were never eligible to vote.  Id.
But the statute does not distinguish between these
situations, and no court has ever agreed with that
interpretation. A person may already have a
disqualifying criminal conviction when she registers,
and so be ineligible from the start, or she may be
eligible when she registers to vote but become
ineligible when later convicted of a crime. Either way,
her removal falls within Congress’s exception for
criminal convictions. Congress simply did not draw a
line based on whether a voter was ineligible from the
start or became ineligible later. The most natural
reading—one adopted by every court to have

8
considered this issue, see, e.g. , Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of
State, 772 F.3d 1335 (11th Cir. 2014) —is that
“ineligible voters” refers simply to anyone on the voter
rolls who is ineligible to vote at the time of removal ,
regardless of whether they were eligible at some point
or not , and  that “any program” refers to any
systematic list maintenance program not covered by
the exceptions.
The RNC also suggests the correct reading of the
statute would undermine states’ ability to maintain
election integrity , RNC Pet’r’s Br. 50 , b ut that
argument ignores  that Congress permits states to
conduct systematic list maintenance programs most of
the time. It bars such programs only during the ninety
days before a federal election , specifically because
systematic list maintenance activities are known to be
error-prone. During  the Quiet Period, voters have a
very limited capacity to address and correct those
errors in time to cast their ballot, and election officials
will have a very limited capacity to make those
corrections—particularly if large numbers of eligible
voters experience these problems at the same time .
Outside that window, the efficiencies of systematic list
maintenance programs may outweigh the costs,
because voters have a meaningful amount of time to
receive notice about a removal and correct any
mistakes made.
That calculus changes, however, in the final days
before a federal election, as reflected in the statute.
Because there is less (or no) time to identify or fix
mistakes, a systematic list maintenance program run
during that window  carries an unacceptable  risk of
disenfranchising eligible voters.  The Quiet Period
thus balances  the NVRA’s twin goals: It permits

9
systematic programs nearly all of the time, but not in
the final ninety days, when protecting eligible voters
must come first.
That judgment is consistent with Congress’s
finding that the right to vote “is a fundamental right,”
52 U.S.C. §  20501(a)(1), and the NVRA’s first stated
goal of “ increas[ing] the number of eligible citizens
who register to vote in elections for Federal office,” 52
U.S.C. § 20501(b)(1).3 And while the statute prohibits
systematic programs during that period (subject to the
narrow exceptions already discussed , 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(B)(i)), that language  allows for non -
systematic—that is, individualized—removals during
that period , see 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
Individualized removals do not present the same risks
because they are “based on individual correspondence
or rigorous individualized inquiry” and thus lead “to a
smaller chance for mistakes.” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346.
Thus, the Quiet Period provision does not prevent a
state from investigating potential noncitizens and
removing them based on individualized information,
even during the Quiet Period . And it nowhere bars
states from using their  resources to ensure
noncitizens are not registered on state voter rolls. All
the statute does is regulate how and when they may
do so.

3 Congress struck a similar balance throughout the NVRA. For
example, Section 8(d)(1)(B)(ii)  of the NVRA does not allow
election officials to remove voters suspected of having moved
outside their jurisdiction from the voter rolls until two general
elections have passed after notice is provided to the voter. This
provision allows election official s to take affirmative steps to
ensure their voter rolls are accurate but requires that the process
permits voters plenty of time to correct any mistakes.

10
Unsurprisingly, the lower federal courts have
agreed that Congress barred system atic removals in
the period before an election because that is when
errors are hardest to correct and the risk is the
greatest. For example, in Arcia v. Florida Secretary of
State, the Eleventh Circuit described the provision as
striking “a careful balance: It permits systematic
removal programs at any time except for the 90 days
before an election because that is when the risk of
disfranchising eligible voters is the greatest.” Arcia,
772 F.3d  at 1346 . The Fourth Circuit’s decision in
Republican National Committee v. North Carolina
State Board of Elections, 120 F.4th 390, 401 (4th Cir.
2024) (quoting Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346 ), adopted the
same reasoning, as have other courts around the
country. See, e.g., Fair Fight Inc. v. True the Vote, 710
F. Supp.  3d 1237, 1243 (N.D. G a. 2024); Majority
Forward v. Ben Hill Cnty . Bd. of Elections,  512 F.
Supp. 3d 1354, 1368 (M.D. G a. 2021); Va. Coal. for
Immigr. Rts. v. Beals, No. 24-2071, 2024 WL 4601052,
at *1 (4th Cir. Oct. 27, 2024) ; Drouillard v. Roberts ,
No. 24-cv-6969, 2024 WL 4667163, at *10 (N.D. Cal.
Nov. 4, 2024) (“The reason Congress chose not to allow
for systematic removal of voters within 90 days of an
election is that ‘[i]n the final days before an
election . . . the calculus changes’ and ‘[e]ligible voters
removed days or weeks before Election Day will likely
not be able to correct the State’s errors in time to
vote.’” (quoting Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346)).
That legislative judgment—that the relative
equities change the closer to an election —is not some
outlier; it is also reflected in this Court’s own election
law precedents . In Purcell v. Gonzalez , 549 U.S. 1
(2006), this Court cautioned against late -breaking

11
changes that leave “ inadequate time to
resolve . . . factual disputes .” Id. at 5 –6. Congress
thought the same. The Quiet Period’s narrow limits
thus ensure that when a state conducts systematic list
maintenance programs—which, as amici discuss
below, are often error -ridden—it leaves itself enough
time to re -enfranchise voters who have been
wrongfully removed. And that judgment holds even
when a state purports to remove only noncitizens.
II. EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE PROVES THAT
SYSTEMATIC VOTER LIST MAINTENANCE
PROGRAMS ARE ERROR-PRONE
The wisdom of Congress’s balanced policy
judgment in the NVRA ’s Quiet Period provision is
borne out by real -world experience. The inherent
limitations in systematic list maintenance programs
lead to errors , with eligible voters removed from the
voter rolls. These programs usually rely on matching
names on voter rolls to names on various government
databases. But those databases are often outdated or
incomplete, and linking different databases often
leads to false positives (i.e., entries that seem to match
but shouldn’t).
These problems are particularly fraught when it
comes to mass determinations about citizenship. And
the impacts are severe even when systematic list
maintenance programs are working as designed.
When matching millions of records, even extremely
low error rates could lead to tens of thousands of false
positives. See Jasleen Singh , Watch Out for False
Voter Fraud Claims Fueled by SAVE Program,
Brennan C tr. for Just . (June 12, 2026) ,
https://perma.cc/6V8A-5JUF. One recurring problem

12
stems from the limitations of the Department of
Homeland Security’s (“DHS”) Systematic Alien
Verification for Entitlements (“SAVE”) database. The
SAVE database’s fallibility is well -documented. See
infra; see also  Jasleen Singh & Spencer Reynolds ,
Homeland Security’s “SAVE” Program Exacerbates
Risks to Voters, Brennan Ctr. for Just. (Jul. 21, 2025),
https://perma.cc/6FME-HBJD (collecting sources) .
Eligible voters subjected to systematic list
maintenance programs aimed at removing
noncitizens have had to resort to litigation to protect
their right to vote. For example, the Arcia case arose
when Florida voters  were wrongfully flagged as
noncitizens because of discrepancies  resulting from
the State’s use of the SAVE database. See 772 F.3d at
1339, 1341.
 The problems are not just with  the SAVE
database. Systematic list maintenance  programs,
which use computerized data-matching processes that
involve matching computerized voter -registration
lists with other computerized data records compiled at
different times and for different reasons , inevitably
lead to errors. That risk, tolerated by the NVRA most
of the time, becomes intolerable during the Quiet
Period because i t takes time to identify and correct
those errors . The examples discussed below confirm
that the potential for errors is pervasive.
A. Alabama
On August 13, 2024, eighty-four days before the
general election, Alabama’s Secretary of State
launched a program targeting 3,251 registered voters
as suspected noncitizens. More than 2,000 of them
were confirmed to have been erroneously flagged and

13
later reactivated. The State confirmed only four
noncitizens; three of whom had never registered at all
and were added to the rolls through a state agency
error; and the fourth said they had never voted.
United State s’ Mot. for Prelim. Inj. 25 n.6, United
States v. Alabama , No. 24 -cv-1329 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 2,
2024), Dkt. No. 12.
Alabama’s 2024  program compared the State’s
voter rolls against driver’s license and ID card data
from the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency (“ALEA”)
and unemployment data from the Alabama
Department of Labor ( “ADOL”). Compl. ¶ 33, United
States v. Alabama, No. 24-cv-1329 (N.D. Ala. Sep. 27,
2024), Dkt. No. 1 . The ALEA data was unreliable.
Driver’s licenses issued to foreign nationals in
Alabama remain valid for up to four years, and non -
driver ID cards for up to eight, and ALEA does not
require newly naturalized citizens to update their
citizenship status bef ore their license or ID card
expires. Id. at ¶¶ 35–37. Because the program did not
distinguish between ALEA records that predated an
individual’s voter registration and those that
postdated it, the State’s program  incorrectly flagged
many naturalized citizens who properly registered to
vote, merely because their license or ID card was not
yet updated. The program made similar errors based
on ADOL records  because ADOL likewise did not
require newly naturalized citizens to update their
records. Id. at ¶¶ 44–47; United State s’ Mot. for
Prelim. Inj. at 8 . The State also ignored
documentation proving voter eligibility: More than
fifty Alabamians flagged as noncitizens by the
program had in fact provided a naturalization or
citizenship certificate to ALEA. United State s’ Mot.

14
for Prelim. Inj. at 7. Secretary Allen’s Chief of Staff,
Wes Helms, testified “that he understood that in any
process using data, you’re going to have the potential
for false positives for other issues.” Prelim. Inj. Hr’g
Tr. at 8:23 –25, United States v. Alabama , No. 24 -cv-
1329 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 16, 2024), Dkt. No. 57.
Many naturalized citizens were thus ensnared.
One of them was Saul Jimenez. Mr. Jimenez had
renewed his foreign national driver’s license shortly
before he became a U.S. citizen in 2022, and he
registered to vote soon after his naturalization
ceremony. Ex. 9: Jimenez Decl. ¶¶ 4, 7, United States
v. Alabama, No. 24 -cv-1329 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 2, 2024),
Dkt. No. 12 -10. Despite being a U.S. citizen, he
received a form letter telling him that his voter
registration had been inactivated and that he would
be removed from the statewide voter list. Id. at ¶¶ 5,
9–11.
Another was Jennifer Berg, a native -born U.S.
citizen who was flagged as a noncitizen. The program
relied on ADOL data, but it appears there were
additional agency paperwork errors: Ms. Berg began
but never completed an online application for
unemployment benefits with ADOL. Yet she was still
targeted under Alabama’s program  because she
purportedly checked a box on that incomplete,
unsubmitted application indicating that she was not a
citizen. In other words, paperwork Ms. Berg had never
even filed was being used to prevent her from
exercising her right to vote. Ex. 11: Berg Decl. ¶¶ 10–
13, United States v. Alabama , No. 24 -cv-1329 (N.D.
Ala. Oct. 2, 2024), Dkt. No. 12 -12. Adding additional
injury, Ms. Berg did not receive a letter from her
county registrar informing her that she had been

15
removed from the voter rolls  until August 29, more
than two weeks after the list maintenance  program
began. United State s’ Mot. for Prelim. Inj. at 9 . A
county registrar incorrectly instructed another
eligible voter, Clarence Hunter, to complete a self -
removal form. Prelim. Inj. Hr’g Tr. at 15:14–25.
None of this was necessary to keep noncitizens off
Alabama’s rolls. The State could have run its program
months earlier, when voters like Mr. Jimenez would
have had time to correct the State’s  mistakes. And
Alabama continues to have “the ability to remove
noncitizens from the rolls on the basis of
individualized information despite the [Quiet Period]
provision,” Prelim. Inj. Hr’g Tr. at 16: 1–10, and the
“authority to investigate and prosecute noncitizens
who try to vote in elections in Alabama,”  id. at 17:2–
10.
B. Virginia
Ninety days before the 2024 General Election,
then-Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin issued
Executive Order 35, which expanded Virginia’s list
maintenance program to require daily updates to the
voter list even during the NVRA Quiet Period. Compl.
¶ 4, Va. Coal. for Immigr. Rts. v. Beals, No. 24-cv-1778
(E.D. Va.  Oct. 7, 2024 ), Dkt. No. 1 . This program
removed individuals who allegedly  had not verif ied
their citizenship status to the Commonwealth’s DMV.
The program required registrars to notify voters of
their pending cancellation and gave them just
fourteen days to provide proof of their citizenship. Id.
¶¶ 2, 4, 37–38.
From the start, the risk of error was clear. Public
reporting quoted one election official in rural Nelson

16
County stating that she had “never encountered a case
of a noncitizen on the voter rolls,” and only knew  of
instances in which the Commonwealth flagged an
alleged noncitizen that turned out to be a legitimate
voter checking the wrong box. Gregory S. Schneider &
Laura Vozzella, Youngkin stokes fears of vast
noncitizen voting in Virginia. Records don’t show it .,
Wash. Post (Oct. 9, 2024) , https://perma.cc/KL98-
2T9N.
In September 2024, Prince William County’s
General Registrar said that while Virginia’s program
had flagged  162 individuals on the voter rolls as
noncitizens from January 2022 to July 2024, at least
forty-three of those 162 individuals were likely
citizens. See McDonald Decl. ¶ 9, Va. Coal. for Immigr.
Rts. v. Beals, No. 24-cv-1778 (E.D. Va. Oct. 15, 2024),
Dkt. No. 26-2. Even so, the Registrar noted that the
Commonwealth’s methodology forced the county to
cancel all of the flagged registrations. Id.
The litigation that resulted revealed even more
errors. Plaintiffs identified several individuals whose
voter registration was erroneously cancelled during
the Quiet Period under Executive Order 35 . One
organization identified eleven individuals who were
removed from the voter rolls because the
Commonwealth concluded they were noncitizens,
even though they were U.S. citizens and eligible voters
who had voted for years . See Suppl. Decl. of Gigi
Traore ¶¶ 4–7, Va. Coal. for Immigr. Rts. v. Beals, No.
24-cv-1778 (E.D. Va. Oct. 24, 2024), Dkt. No. 108.
One was Christine Rabassa . Ms. Rabassa, a
native-born U.S.  citizen and eligible voter who had
voted in Virginia elections for over twenty years, had

17
her registration cancelled during the Quiet Period,
apparently because her driver’s license expired. When
she attempted to vote during early voting, poll
workers were unable to locate her in the poll books
and she was informed that her registration had been
cancelled. She was denied the opportunity to vote that
day because of the unlawful removal. Ultimately, Ms.
Rabassa was allowed to re-register. See Suppl. Decl. of
Anna J. Dorman  ¶¶ 3–16, Va. Coal. for Immigr. Rts.
v. Beals, No. 24-cv-1778 (E.D. Va. Oct. 24, 2024), Dkt.
No. 108-2.
Another voter , Shantae Martin, had a similar
story. Ms. Martin was born and raised in Virginia and
had been registered to vote for over ten years .
Virginia’s list maintenance p rogram erroneously
identified her as a noncitizen . She also went to the
Virginia DMV to get her driver’s license, which
appeared to have prompted the unlawful removal. See
id. at ¶¶ 17–28.
Ms. Rabassa and Ms. Martin should have never
been removed from the rolls, but other voters likely
fared worse. Ms. Rabassa was able to re-register only
because she had tried early voting; had she gone on
Election Day, she would have been denied the
opportunity to vote a regular ballot in the election. Ms.
Martin learned that her registration had been
cancelled only because one of the plaintiff
organizations in that suit, African Communities
Together, informed her . Other eligible voters
ensnared in the systematic program, by contrast, may
not have learned of the error in time.

18
C. Texas
In January 2019, Texas’s Secretary of State
announced that his office had “discovered” 95,000
noncitizens who had a matching voter registration
record—a claim amplified by Texas Attorney General
Ken Paxton, Texas Governor Greg Abbott, and
eventually Presid ent Donald J. Trump . See 3d Am.
Compl. ¶¶ 122–27, Tex. League of United Latin Am.
Citizens v. Whitley , No. 19 -cv-74 (W.D. Tex. Mar . 6,
2019), Dkt. No. 97 (citation modified). The Secretary
of State transmitted those names to counties , and
many of the counties immediately initiated processes
to remove those voters from the rolls.
However, just four days after that announcement,
the Secretary of State’s office began informing county
officials that its list of suspected noncitizen voters
“may be flawed,” and that some voters on the list
“shouldn’t be there because they had already proven
their citizenship.” Id. at ¶ 135 (citation modified).
The scale of the error soon became apparent . In
Harris County alone, 18,000 individuals on the
Secretary of State’s list “had already been identified
as citizens” and “Harris County expected more
mistakes to be discovered.” Id. at ¶ 141 (citation
modified). The same was true across the State . See,
e.g., id. at ¶ 142 (in McLennan County, all voters on
the Secretary of State’s list were U.S. citizens);  id. at
¶ 143 (in Williamson County,  the county
administrator reported that the Secretary of State
determined more than half the original list of county
voters were citizens). Among other obvious problems,
the Secretary of State’s list contained naturalized
citizens who registered to vote after they became U.S.

19
citizens. See id. at ¶ 146. Notwithstanding all those
errors, the State continued purging voters from the
rolls based on the list. See id. at ¶ 149.
Voters brought suit for relief from this very
expansive Texas list maintenance effort. Their stories
illustrate well why systematic efforts to remove
alleged noncitizens inevitably ensnare many U.S.
citizens (especially naturalized citizens) who are
eligible voters . Julieta Garibay, a naturalized U.S.
citizen and resident of Travis County was wrongfully
identified as a noncitizen, and her information was
sent to Travis County . Travis County notified her in
writing that “it would investigate her U.S.
citizenship.” Id. at ¶ 10. Another plaintiff —also a
naturalized U.S. citizen —was told by the Smith
County Elections Administrator’s office that he had
thirty days to “provide proof of citizenship” or “his
voter registration [would] be cancelled.” Id. at ¶ 30.
The same happened to Elena Keane, Maria Felicitas
Barbosa, and several other plaintiffs—all naturalized
citizens—who were told by their respective counties
that if they failed to provide proof of citizenship within
thirty days, their registration would be cancelled. See
id. at ¶¶ 16–42. Travis County officials told at least
one voter—Martine Hummel, a naturalized citizen —
that she should cancel her voter registration to get off
the suspect-voter list. See id. at ¶ 45.
In the years since, Texas has continued efforts to
systematically remove noncitizens from its voter rolls,
and those efforts have continued to ensnare U.S.
citizens. In October 2025, the Texas Secretary of State
announced that her office had compared the State’s
voter registration list against the SAVE database to
identify 2,724 potential noncitizens who are registered

20
to vote in Texas . See Jen Fifield & Zach Despart, A
federal tool to check voter citizenship keeps making
mistakes. It led to confusion in Texas, Tex. Trib. (Feb.
13, 2026) , https://perma.cc/W7J9-M3FX. This effort
involved conducting list maintenance using the SAVE
database, which had recently been upd ated by DHS.
Id.
This effort again ensnared many U.S . citizens.
Among them were four registered voters who
challenged the use of the modified SAVE database in
League of Women Voters v. U.S. Dep artment of
Homeland Security, 835 F. Supp. 3d 79 (D.D.C. 2026).
As the district court found , their sworn declarations

inaccurate [Social Security Administration  (“SSA”)]

required to confirm their citizenship to maintain their
voter registrations.” Id. at 113. When this Court
stayed the injunction in that case for unrelated
reasons, it recognized that for at least one of those

D. Iowa
On October 22, 2024, just before the federal
election, Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate sent
county registrars a list of thousands of voters he
claimed were noncitizens. See Robin Opsahl, Iowa
Secretary of State says 87 noncitizens voted in
elections, Iowa Cap . Dispatch (Oct. 22, 2024) ,
https://perma.cc/T5FC-PD7U. He directed registrars
to distribute the names to precincts so poll workers
could challenge ballots cast by anyone on the list. The
list was compiled from State driver’s license records,
many of which included  out-of-date data regarding
citizenship status.  For example, one voter who
registered in 2022 was flagged as a noncitizen based
on information she provided to the Department of
Transportation in 2000. See Selcuk v. Pate, No. 24-cv-
390, 2024 WL 5054961, at *8 (S.D. Iowa Nov. 3, 2024).
In total, Secretary Pate’s list included 2,176
registered voters.  Id. at *1 . But his staff later
admitted in litigation that at least eighty-eight
percent of those listed were eligible citizens. See
Suppl. Decl. of Michael Ross ¶ 36, Selcuk v. Pate, No.
24-cv-390 (S.D. Iowa  Nov. 2, 2024 ), Dkt. No. 31 -1.
Even so, Secretary Pate’s directive required poll
workers to challenge ballots cast by anyone on the list,
even if they presented citizenship documentation or
poll workers otherwise knew they were eligible. See
Selcuk, 2024 WL 5054961, at *7 –8 (“[L]ocal officials
are being directed to lodge a challenge to voter

24
eligibility based on non-citizenship even if the officials
have personal knowledge that the voters are United
States citizens (or, at least, do not believe there is
reasonable suspicion to conclude otherwise).”). After
the ACLU and ACLU of Iowa filed suit, Secretary Pate
backed do wn from the mandatory language of his
order and advised officials not to challenge ballots of
voters that they knew to be citizens. See id. at *8.
Although it was a directive to challenge ballots,
rather than to cancel voters’ registrations, Iowa’s lastminute list maintenance  program demonstrates the
need for the Quiet Period prior to an election. The
program came just two weeks  before Election Day,
when early voting was already underway. Such a
program on the eve of an election inevitably risks
voter confusion, meritless challenges, and potential
disenfranchisement.
E. Arizona
The experience in Arizona is particularly relevant
here and demonstrates that the State’s use of the
SAVE database has led to mass misidentifications of
eligible voters as noncitizens. See Sasha Hupka,
Maricopa County investigated 60 suspected noncitizen
voters. 52 are citizens, 8 are not ., Votebeat Ariz. (Sep.
28, 2026) , https://perma.cc/8U7K-SR9E. After
systematic list maintenance using the SAVE database
was performed, Maricopa County Recorder Justin
Heap originally flagged 207 individuals as alleged
noncitizens on the voter rolls. Maricopa Cnty. Att’y’s
Off., Statement from MCAO on Referrals from the
Maricopa County Recorder's Office  (Mar. 23, 2026) ,
https://perma.cc/V5AZ-CGWP. Heap asked the
county’s top prosecutor to investigate sixty of these

25
individuals who had allegedly voted.  Id. The
prosecutor, County Attorney Rachel Mitchell,
ultimately determined that only eight of these
individuals are noncitizens. Mitchell determined that
of the eight noncitizens, all but one were erroneously
registered by the county while renewing their driver’s
licenses. Hupka, Maricopa County investigated 60
suspected noncitizen voters. 52 are citizens, 8 are not ..
Thus, in a county with 2.5 million registered voters,
this list maintenance effort found only eight
noncitizens who had voted; seven of  whom had been
registered through the county’s own error.  Id. As Ms.
Mitchell acknowledged, the number of ballots cast by
noncitizens was too small to sway any election. Id.
III. IT IS EX CEEDINGLY RARE FOR
NONCITIZENS TO BE ON VOTER ROLLS.
Recent state audits have shown that incidents of
noncitizen voting continue to be rare, isolated
occurrences, and the number of potential noncitizens
identified is negligible. For example, of the 35 million
registered voters evaluated recently by seven states
using the recently modified SAVE database, only
0.01% of all registered voters  in these state s were
identified as likely noncitizens. Fifield & Despart, A
federal tool to check voter citizenship keeps making
mistakes. It led to confusion in Texas .5 Moreover,

5 See also Stephen Richer, Another Data Point Against the Theory
That Noncitizens Are Voting En Masse , Cato Inst ., (May 14,
2026), https://perma.cc/HK89-HD45 (noting Utah’s recent audit
of 2.1 million voters that identified one noncitizen registered and
Pennsylvania’s audit of 210,905 voters that identified one
noncitizen registered who never voted, is no longer registered,
and no longer lives in Pennsylvania).

26
evidence shows that almost all noncitizens found on
voter rolls end ed up there accidentally, as the result
of administrative errors and confusion.  Pam Fessler,
Some Noncitizens Do Wind Up Registered to Vote, But
Usually Not on Purpose , Nat ’l Pub. Radio, (Feb.  26,
2019), https://perma.cc/ZY98-QX6N.
Another recent analysis of claims of noncitizen
voting showed that even “the largest claims never
identify a number of possible noncitizens registrants
or voter that amount to more than roughly one -tenth
of one percent of the number of active registered
voters in a s tate.” See Claims of Noncitizen
Registration or Voting: Analysis and Tracker , Ctr. for
Election Innovation & Rsch . (Sep. 2026) ,
https://perma.cc/9SPL-4UCS; see also  Wren Orey  et
al., Four Things to Know About Noncitizen Voting ,
Bipartisan Pol ’y C tr. (Jul. 22, 2026 ),
https://perma.cc/Y9EL-A4VQ (finding that nationwide
“just 0.04% of voter verification cases are returned as
noncitizens”). Or they ultimately do not  find any
confirmed noncitizens. The New York Times recently
reported that in August of this year, DHS sent Nevada
a list of 185 purported noncitizens who were
registered to vote on Nevada’s voter rolls. Nick
Corasaniti, From 16,000 to 185 to Zero: Trump’s
Claims of Illegal Voting in Nevada Fizzle, N.Y. Times
(Sep. 24, 2026) , https://perma.cc/6CHC-2AZ9.
According to the Times, Nevada confirmed a month
later that every single person on DHS’s list was a
lawfully registered citizen.
Many states are regularly searching for
noncitizens through large systematic list maintenance
programs, despite the overwhelming evidence that
noncitizen voting is extremely rare, and that these

27
systematic list maintenance programs sweep up large
numbers of U.S. citizens. Most of the time, states are
free to do so, whether or not it is good policy or a wise
use of resources. But under the NVRA, they may not
do it during the Quiet Period.
*     *     *
There is no question that states have not only the
authority but the responsibility to protect the
integrity of their elections by conducting routine list
maintenance activities as provided by the NVRA.
Williams v. Rhodes , 393 U.S. 23, 34 (1968)  (“[T]he
State is left with broad powers to regulate voting,
which may include laws relating to the qualification[s]
and functions of electors.”). But conducting systemic
list maintenance activities so close to an election
provides too great a risk that eligible citizens will be
ensnared in these activities with too little time to
remedy any errors by the state.
The Court should uphold the careful balance
Congress struck in the plain language of the NVRA.

28
CONCLUSION
The judgment below should be affirmed.
